headline: Sequence models and assemblies map regulatory elements and selection footprints
label: Computational Functional Genomics Inference
summary: Recent work pairs high-quality assemblies and deep learning models with regulatory and selection inference across species and tissues.
synthesis: The common thread is computational inference of functional and evolutionary structure directly from genome sequence, haplotypes, and expression data. Several items apply learned sequence models: a CNN enhancer predictor trained on re-analyzed Heliconius wing ATAC-seq and histone ChIP data reaches AUROC 0.909, and SHADES uses multi-scale haplotype variation to distinguish neutrality, sweeps, balancing selection, and related processes. Assembly-driven work supports this scale of analysis: a haplotype-resolved 32 Gb axolotl genome, combined with multi-genome alignment, identifies more than 523,000 conserved non-coding elements. Other items extend the approach to expression and population data. eModule quantifies eRNA from GTEx RNA-seq and finds sex bias in 47% of active enhancers across 41 tissues, many primate-specific. scEvoSel overlays population selection scores (DCMS) onto scRNA-seq atlases to locate selection-relevant cell types in pig and chicken. Ridge models on k-mer features from canine buccal and cell-free DNA predict age, with stronger age-linked sequence features in buccal DNA. What is new is the extension of these inference approaches across sequence-level, haplotype-level, and single-cell readouts.
